questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Activity of a radioactive sample decreases to $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{th}$ of its original value in 4 days. Then in 16 days its activity will become $x$ times the original value. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Let the initial activity be $A_0$ and the half-life be $T_{1/2}$.

The activity after time $t$ is given by $A = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$.

Given that $A = \dfrac{A_0}{4}$ at $t = 4$ days:

$\dfrac{A_0}{4} = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{4}{T_{1/2}}}$

$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{4}{T_{1/2}}}$

$\dfrac{4}{T_{1/2}} = 2 \Rightarrow T_{1/2} = 2$ days.

After $t = 16$ days, the activity $A'$ is:

$A' = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{16}{2}} = A_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8 = \dfrac{A_0}{256}$

Thus, the activity becomes $\dfrac{1}{256}$ times the original value, so $x = \dfrac{1}{256}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{256}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive element has rate of disintegration $16{,}000$ disintegrations per minute at a particular instant. After four minutes, it becomes $2000$ disintegrations per minute. The decay constant per minute is
questions.solution:
The rate of disintegration (activity) of a radioactive element follows the exponential decay law:

$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

Given initial activity $A_0 = 16000$ disintegrations per minute, final activity $A = 2000$ disintegrations per minute, and time $t = 4$ minutes.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$2000 = 16000 e^{-\lambda (4)}$

$\dfrac{2000}{16000} = e^{-4\lambda}$

$\dfrac{1}{8} = e^{-4\lambda}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) = -4\lambda$

$\log_e(2^{-3}) = -4\lambda$

$-3 \log_e 2 = -4\lambda$

$\lambda = \dfrac{3}{4} \log_e 2$

$\lambda = 0.75 \log_e 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive sample has half-life of $5$ years. The percentage of fraction decayed in $10$ years will be
questions.solution:
Given half-life $T_{1/2} = 5$ years and time $t = 10$ years.

Number of half-lives $n = \dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$

Fraction of sample remaining after $n$ half-lives is given by $\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$

$\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Fraction of sample decayed $= 1 - \dfrac{N}{N_0} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Percentage of fraction decayed $= \dfrac{3}{4} \times 100\% = 75\%$

Answer: $75\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two samples A and B contain equal amount of radioactive substances. If $\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)^{th}$ of sample A and $\left(\dfrac{1}{128}\right)^{th}$ of sample B, remain after 9 hours, then the ratio of half life period of B to that of A is
questions.solution:
Let the initial amount of both samples be $N_0$.

The amount of radioactive substance remaining after time $t$ is given by $N = N_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$.

For sample A, after $t = 9$ hours:

$\dfrac{N_0}{8} = N_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{9}{T_A}}$

$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{9}{T_A}}$

$\dfrac{9}{T_A} = 3 \Rightarrow T_A = 3$ hours.

For sample B, after $t = 9$ hours:

$\dfrac{N_0}{128} = N_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{9}{T_B}}$

$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^7 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{9}{T_B}}$

$\dfrac{9}{T_B} = 7 \Rightarrow T_B = \dfrac{9}{7}$ hours.

The ratio of the half-life period of B to that of A is:

$\dfrac{T_B}{T_A} = \dfrac{\dfrac{9}{7}}{3} = \dfrac{3}{7}$

Answer: $3:7$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample is measured as $N_0$ counts per minute at time $t = 0$ and $\dfrac{N_0}{e}$ counts per minute at time $t = 3$ minute. The time (in minute) in which the activity reduces to half the value, is
questions.solution:
The activity of a radioactive sample at time $t$ is given by $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.

Given that at $t = 0$, $A = N_0$.

At $t = 3$ minutes, $A = \dfrac{N_0}{e}$.

Substituting these values into the decay equation:

$\dfrac{N_0}{e} = N_0 e^{-3\lambda}$

$e^{-1} = e^{-3\lambda}$

Comparing the powers of $e$, we get:

$3\lambda = 1 \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ min}^{-1}$

The time in which the activity reduces to half its initial value is the half-life $T_{1/2}$, which is given by:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\log_e 2}{\lambda}$

Substituting the value of $\lambda$:

$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\log_e 2}{\dfrac{1}{3}} = 3 \log_e 2 \text{ min}$

Answer: $3\log_e 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The half-life of the isotope ${}_{11}\text{Na}^{24}$ is 15 hr. How much time does it take for $\left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^{\text{th}}$ of a sample of this isotope to decay ?
questions.solution:
Fraction of the sample decayed is $\dfrac{7}{8}$.

Fraction of the sample remaining is $1 - \dfrac{7}{8} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

The amount of substance remaining after time $t$ is given by $N = N_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$.

Substituting the values, we get $\dfrac{1}{8} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{15}}$.

$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\dfrac{t}{15}}$

$\dfrac{t}{15} = 3$

$t = 45$ hr.

Answer: $45$ hour

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the density of oxygen nucleus $({}^{16}_{8}\text{O})$ and helium nucleus $({}^{4}_{2}\text{He})$ is
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus with mass number $A$ is given by $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.

The volume of the nucleus is $V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3 A$.

The mass of the nucleus is $M \approx A m$, where $m$ is the average mass of a nucleon.

The density of the nucleus is $\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{A m}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{m}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3}$.

Since the density is independent of the mass number $A$, it is constant for all nuclei.

Therefore, the ratio of the density of the oxygen nucleus to the helium nucleus is $1 : 1$.

Answer: $1 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two different radioactive elements with half lives $T_1$ and $T_2$ have undecayed atoms $N_1$ and $N_2$ respectively, present at a given instant. The ratio of their activities at this instant is
questions.solution:
Activity of a radioactive element is given by $A = \lambda N$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is related to half-life $T$ as $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T}$

For the first element, activity $A_1 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_1} N_1$

For the second element, activity $A_2 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_2} N_2$

The ratio of their activities is $\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\ln 2}{T_1} N_1}{\dfrac{\ln 2}{T_2} N_2} = \dfrac{N_1 T_2}{N_2 T_1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{N_1 T_2}{N_2 T_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive element having half-life 30 min . is undergoing beta decay. The fraction of radioactive element remains undecayed after 90 min . will be
questions.solution:
The fraction of radioactive material remaining after time $t$ is determined by the decay formula:

$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$

Given a half-life $T_{1/2} = 30\ \text{min}$ and time $t = 90\ \text{min}$, the elapsed time spans $3$ half-lives.

Substituting into the decay law yields:

$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$

The fraction remaining undecayed is therefore $\frac{1}{8}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two radioactive materials ' $M_1{ }^{\prime}$ and ' $M_2{ }^{\prime}$ have decay constants ' $9 \lambda$ ' and ' $\lambda$ ' respectively. Initially they have the same number of nuclei. The ratio of the number of nuclei of $M_1$ to that of $M_2$ will be ' $\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{\prime}$ after a time interval
questions.solution:
Given initial nuclei count $N_0$ for both materials, their quantities follow exponential decay: $N_1(t) = N_0 e^{-9\lambda t}$ for $M_1$ and $N_2(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ for $M_2$, where $t$ is time.

The condition $\frac{N_1(t)}{N_2(t)} = \frac{1}{e}$ leads to $\frac{e^{-9\lambda t}}{e^{-\lambda t}} = e^{-1}$, simplifying to $e^{-8\lambda t} = e^{-1}$.

Equating exponents gives $-8\lambda t = -1$, so $t = \frac{1}{8\lambda}$.

The ratio becomes $\frac{1}{e}$ at time $t = \frac{1}{8\lambda}$, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radio active element has rate of disintegration 8000 disintegrations per minute at a particular instant. After four minutes it becomes 2000 disintegrations per minute. The decay constant per minute is
questions.solution:
The rate of radioactive disintegration follows exponential decay: $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.

Given $R_0 = 8000$ and $R = 2000$ after $t = 4$ minutes, we solve for $\lambda$:

$2000 = 8000 e^{-4\lambda}$

Simplifying gives $\frac{1}{4} = e^{-4\lambda}$.

Taking natural logarithms: $\ln\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = -4\lambda$

Expanding: $-\ln 4 = -4\lambda$

Thus $\lambda = \frac{\ln 4}{4} = \frac{\ln (2^2)}{4} = \frac{1}{2} \ln 2$

This matches option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive element has rate of disintegration 9000 disintegration per minute at a particular instant. After two minutes it becomes 3000 disintegration per minute. The decay constant per minute is
questions.solution:
The radioactive decay formula $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ relates the disintegration rate $R$ at time $t$ to the initial rate $R_0$ and decay constant $\lambda$.

Given $R_0 = 9000$ disintegrations/min, $R = 3000$ disintegrations/min at $t = 2$ min:

$3000 = 9000 e^{-2\lambda}$

Simplifying gives $\frac{1}{3} = e^{-2\lambda}$

Taking natural logarithms of both sides:

$\ln\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = -2\lambda$

Using the logarithmic identity $\ln\left(\frac{1}{a}\right) = -\ln(a)$:

$-\ln(3) = -2\lambda$

Solving for $\lambda$ yields:

$\lambda = \frac{\ln(3)}{2}$

This matches option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A radioactive element ${ }_{92}^{242} \mathrm{X}$ emits two $\alpha$ particles, one electron and two positrons. The product nucleus is represented by ${ }_{\mathrm{P}}^{234} \mathrm{Y}$. The value of P is
questions.solution:
Determining the atomic number $P$ follows from applying the rules of radioactive decay to the transformation ${ }_{92}^{242} \mathrm{X} \to { }_{P}^{234} \mathrm{Y}$.

An $\alpha$ decay reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2. After two $\alpha$ emissions, the mass number becomes $242 - 2 \times 4 = 234$ and the atomic number becomes $92 - 2 \times 2 = 88$.

A $\beta^-$ decay leaves the mass number unchanged and increases the atomic number by 1. After this emission, the atomic number becomes $88 + 1 = 89$.

A $\beta^+$ decay leaves the mass number unchanged and decreases the atomic number by 1. After two such decays, the atomic number becomes $89 - 2 \times 1 = 87$.

Since the final nucleus is ${ }_{P}^{234} \mathrm{Y}$, where the mass number 234 matches our result, the atomic number is $P = 87$.

$\boxed{87}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The activity of radioactive sample is measured as $\mathrm{N}_0$ counts per minute at time $\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{o}$, and $\frac{\mathrm{N}_0}{\mathrm{e}}$ counts per minute at time $\mathrm{t}=3$ minute, The activity reduces to half its value in time (in minute)
questions.solution:
The activity follows radioactive decay: $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$.

Given $A = \frac{N_0}{e}$ when $t = 3$ minutes, substitution yields:

$\frac{N_0}{e} = N_0 e^{-3\lambda}$

Simplification gives $e^{-1} = e^{-3\lambda}$, from which $\lambda = \frac{1}{3}$ per minute.

The half-life is $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 3 \ln 2$ minutes, matching option B.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A radioactive element A decays into radioactive element C by the following processes in succession.
$\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{~B}+{ }_2 \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{e}}^4 ; \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$
Then elements
questions.solution:
Analyzing the radioactive decay chain of element $A = _Z^M A$:

Alpha decay: $A \rightarrow B + _2^4 \text{He}$
By conservation: mass number $M = M_B + 4 \Rightarrow M_B = M - 4$
Atomic number $Z = Z_B + 2 \Rightarrow Z_B = Z - 2$
Thus $B = _{Z-2}^{M-4} B$

Beta decay (2$\beta^-$): $B \rightarrow C + 2\ _{-1}^0 e$
Mass number: $M - 4 = M_C$
Atomic number: $Z - 2 = Z_C - 2 \Rightarrow Z_C = Z$
Thus $C = _Z^{M-4} C$

$A$ and $C$ share atomic number $Z$ but differ in mass number ($M$ vs. $M-4$), confirming they are isotopes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: ${ }_{88} \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{a}}^{226}$ is converted into ${ }_{82} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{b}}^{206}$ by emission of alpha $(\alpha)$ and beta $(\beta)$ particles. The number of alpha and beta particles emitted are respectively
questions.solution:
The nuclear decay from _{88}\mathrm{Ra}^{226}$ to _{82}\mathrm{Pb}^{206}$ involves emission of $x$ alpha particles (_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}$) and $y$ beta particles (_{-1}\mathrm{e}^{0}$).

Mass number conservation gives $226 = 206 + 4x$, reducing to $4x = 20$ and $x = 5$.

Atomic number conservation yields $88 = 82 + 2x - y$. Substituting $x = 5$ gives $88 = 82 + 10 - y$, so $y = 92 - 88 = 4$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two radioactive materials A and B having decay constant '7 $\lambda$ ' and ' $\lambda$ ' respectively, initially have same number of nuclei. The time taken to have the ratio of number of nuclei of material B to that of A as ' e ' is
questions.solution:
Let $N_A(t)$ and $N_B(t)$ denote the number of nuclei of materials A and B at time $t$, with initial quantity $N_0$ for both. The decay follows $N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, where the decay constants are $\lambda_A = 7\lambda$ and $\lambda_B = \lambda$.

Thus, $N_A(t) = N_0 e^{-7\lambda t}$ and $N_B(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. Given the ratio condition:

$\frac{N_B(t)}{N_A(t)} = e$

Substituting the expressions yields:

$\frac{N_0 e^{-\lambda t}}{N_0 e^{-7\lambda t}} = e^{6\lambda t} = e$

Equating exponents gives $6\lambda t = 1$, so $t = \frac{1}{6\lambda}$, corresponding to option B.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
For the following reaction, the particle ' $x$ ' is
${ }_6^{\mathrm{C}^{11}} \longrightarrow{ }_5^{\mathrm{B}^{11}}+\beta^{+}+\mathrm{X}$
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction ${}_6^{11}\mathrm{C} \to {}_5^{11}\mathrm{B} + \beta^+ + X$ requires identifying the unknown particle X by applying conservation laws.

Mass number conservation gives $11 = 11 + 0 + A_X$, yielding $A_X = 0$.

Atomic number conservation gives $6 = 5 + 1 + Z_X$, yielding $Z_X = 0$.

The particle with $A=0$ and $Z=0$ corresponds to a neutrino. In positron emission, a proton converts to a neutron, positron, and electron neutrino: ${}_Z^A X \to {}_{Z-1}^A Y + {}_1^0e + \nu_e$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two radioactive substances $A$ and $B$ have decay constants ' $5 \lambda$ ' and ' $\lambda$ ' respectively. At $\mathrm{t}=0$, they have the same number of nuclei. The ratio of number of nuclei of A to those of B will be $\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}\right)^2$ after a time interval
questions.solution:
Number of nuclei remained after time $t$ can be written as $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{N}_0 \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \mathrm{t}}\mathrm{N}_1=\mathrm{N}_0 \mathrm{e}^{-5 \lambda \mathrm{t}}...(i)$
and $\mathrm{N}_2=\mathrm{N}_0 \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \mathrm{t}}$...(ii)
Dividing equation (i) by equation (ii), we get,
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{N_1}{N_2}=e^{(-5 \lambda+\lambda) t}=e^{-4 \lambda t}=\frac{1}{e^{4 \lambda t}} \\
& \frac{N_1}{N_2}=\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^2=\frac{1}{e^2} ...[Given]\\
\therefore \quad & \frac{1}{e^2}=\frac{1}{e^{4 \lambda t}} \\
\therefore \quad & 2=4 \lambda t \Rightarrow t=\frac{2}{4 \lambda}=\frac{1}{2 \lambda}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Two different radioactive elements with half-lives ' $\mathrm{T}_{1}$ ' and ' $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ ' have undecayed
atoms ' $\mathrm{N}_{1}{ }^{\prime}$ and ${ }^{\prime} \mathrm{N}_{2}{ }^{\prime}$ respectively, present at a given instant. The ratio of their
activities at this instant is
questions.solution:
Activity, $\mathrm{R}\left(=\frac{\mathrm{dN}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)=\lambda \mathrm{N}$
Decay constant $\lambda=\frac{\log _{e} 2}{\mathrm{~T}}\therefore$ Activity $R=\frac{\left(\log _{\mathrm{e}} 2\right) \mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{T}}\therefore \mathrm{R}_{1}=\frac{\left(\log _{e} 2\right) \mathrm{N}_{1}}{\mathrm{~T}_{1}}, \mathrm{R}_{2}=\frac{\left(\log _{e} 2\right) \mathrm{N}_{2}}{\mathrm{~T}_{2}}$
For two elements $\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\frac{N_{1}}{T_{1}} \times \frac{T_{2}}{N_{2}}=\left(\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\right)=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)$

questions.q: An ' $\alpha$ ' particle of energy $10 \mathrm{eV}$ is moving in a circular path in uniform magnetic field. The energy of proton moving in the same path and same magnetic field will be [mass of ' $\alpha$ ' particle $=4$ times mass of proton $]$
questions.solution:
(C)
From the formula mentioned above, momentum of particle moving in a magnetic field $\mathrm{mv}=\mathrm{p}=\mathrm{qBr}$
Therefore, Kinetic Energy of that particle can be written as $\mathrm{KE}=\frac{\mathrm{p}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{~m}}=\frac{q^{2} B^{2} r^{2}}{2 m}$
In the same magnetic field for the same path, $\mathrm{KE} \propto \frac{\mathrm{q}^{2}}{\mathrm{~m}}$
This ratio is same for the alpha particle and the proton. $\left(\frac{(2 \mathrm{e})^{2}}{4 \mathrm{amu}}=\frac{4 \mathrm{e}^{2}}{4 \mathrm{amu}}=\right.\frac{\mathrm{e}^{2}}{\mathrm{amu}}$; Here amu is the atomic mass unit)
So, in such conditions, both will have the same energy. Hence, energy of the alpha particle will be $8 \mathrm{eV}$ too.

questions.q: A radioactive nucleus emits $4 \alpha$ particles and $7 \beta$ particles in succession. The ratio of number of neutrons to that of protons is $[\mathrm{A}=$ mass number, $\mathrm{Z}=$ atomic number $]$
questions.solution:
Let us assume, a particle $X$ having atomic number $Z$ and mass number $A$.
When an a-particle is emitted by a nucleus, then its atomic number decreases by 2 and mass number decreases by 4 . So, for given case, $\mathrm{Z} \mathrm{X}^{\mathrm{A}} \stackrel{4 \text { a-particle }}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{Z}_{-\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{Y}^{\mathrm{A}-16}$
When a $\beta$-particle is emitted by a nucleus its atomic number increases by one and mass number remains unchanged. So, for given case,
$\mathrm{Z}-8 \mathrm{Y}^{\mathrm{A}-16} \stackrel{7 \beta-p a r t i c l e}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{Z}-1 \mathrm{Z}^{\mathrm{A}-16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In radioactive decay process, the negatively charged emitted $\beta$ -particles are
options: the electrons present inside the nucleus
the electrons produced as a result of the decay of neutrons inside the nucleus
the electrons produced as a result of collisions between atoms
the electrons orbiting around the nucleus
questions.solution: Beta decay can involve the emission of either electrons or positrons. The electrons or positrons emitted in a $\beta$ -decay do not exist inside the nucleus. They are only created at the time of emission, just as photons are created when an atom makes a transition from higher to a lower energy state. In negative $\beta$ -decay a neutron in the nucleus is transformed into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Hence, in radioactive decay process, the negatively charged emitted \beta-particles are the electrons produced as a result of the decay of neutrons present inside the nucleus.

questions.q: A particle having almost zero mass and exactly zero charge is
questions.solution:
We know that the neutrino is the particle which has almost zero mass and exactly zero charge. Positron has the charge $+e$ and mass $m_{e}$ [equal to electron mass].
Electron is a particle which has $-e$ charge and $9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg mass.
Neutron is a particle which has zero charge and $1838 \mathrm{~m}_{e}$ mass.
So, the required answer is neutrino.
